intro: The cycle opens in G major with a tune over triplets. The same eight bars are heard four times in this performance, so the changes lie in what surrounds them. All thirteen pieces of this set are played by Donald Betts.
question: How does an eight-bar tune survive being heard four times?

sections.label: A · opening strain, played twice
sections.mNote: eight bars in G major, repeated literally

sections.label: B · six new bars, slowing to a fermata
A′ · the opening tune returns
sections.mNote: the eight bars come back to close the strain

sections.label: B · second strain repeated
sections.mNote: new bars and returning tune heard again

cues.title: A tune over triplets
cues.text: Two beats to the bar in G major, marked p. The tune leaps from B up to G and steps down F♯–E–D. Beneath it, triplet quavers in broken chords weave between the hands, with the pedal marked and the bass marking the beats separately.
cues.evidence: First edition p. 3 (IMSLP #03060): G major, 2/4, p, triplet groups marked “3” in the inner voices, pedal in bar 1; melodic notes B–G–F♯–E–D checked against the Mutopia transcription (SchumannOp15No01.ly). The report reads G major from 0:05 (local key r = 0.85–0.93); the level rises from −17.9 dB at 0:00 to −10.1 dB at 0:05.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The eight bars again
cues.text: The opening eight bars are repeated, as the repeat sign requires. The second pass comes back at the same pace with the same accompaniment; the long note that closes bar 8 is where the join can be heard.
cues.evidence: The form analysis matches 0:03–0:16 with 0:20–0:34 (lag 17.5 s, mean similarity 0.92); the report shows a boundary at 0:18 (novelty 0.54). The score has a repeat sign after bar 8 and a minim at the end of the bar.

cues.title: Slowing before the tune returns
cues.text: The second strain opens with six new bars marked piano. The last carries a ritardando and a fermata, so the music almost stops before the opening tune comes back. In the recording the level dips around 0:50.
cues.evidence: Score p. 3: ritardando and fermata in the sixth bar after the repeat sign, then piano and the opening tune. Report: −8.7 dB at 0:45, −14.5 dB at 0:50, novelty 0.72 at 0:50. The form analysis finds 0:55–1:10 resembling 0:20–0:35 (mean 0.96), the returning tune.

cues.title: Written in February 1838
cues.text: Schumann’s diary records work on the Kinderszenen by Saturday 17 February 1838; on the 22nd he played from them to a merchant visiting from Bremen. Clara Wieck was giving recitals in Vienna that winter, and in March he wrote to tell her of the pieces.
cues.evidence: Diary entries quoted in the Robert-Schumann-Haus Zwickau catalogue 175 Jahre Kinderszenen (2013), item 1; the March letter is item 3 (17 March 1838). Clara’s Vienna recitals ran from December 1837 to April 1838 (Nancy Reich, Clara Schumann, rev. edn).

cues.title: The one complete autograph
cues.text: Only this piece of the thirteen survives in a complete autograph, now in the Robert-Schumann-Haus, Zwickau. Schumann dedicated it in 1847 to his sister-in-law Marie Wieck. No manuscript of the whole set is known.
cues.evidence: Zwickau catalogue 175 Jahre Kinderszenen, item 5 (autograph 3702–A1, dedicated 1847 to Marie Wieck); the Henle Urtext review at schumann-portal.de/3213.html says there was probably never a continuous autograph.

transitions.title: The repeat ends and a new strain begins
transitions.how: After the second pass of the eight-bar strain the repeat sign is not taken again. Bar 9 begins a new strain marked p, with a different melodic shape over the continuing triplet motion. The pulse and the metre are unchanged, so the join is a change of material rather than of tempo.
transitions.evidence: The form analysis places the repeat of 0:03–0:16 at 0:20–0:34, so the second pass ends near 0:36; the report shows novelty 0.40 at 0:36. The first edition (p. 3) has the repeat sign after bar 8 and p at bar 9.

transitions.title: A fermata, then the tune comes home
transitions.how: The sixth new bar carries a ritardando and a fermata, which holds the music almost still. The next bar is marked p and the opening tune returns note for note, in G major, to close the strain. The pause makes the return sound like an arrival: the listener has heard the same eight bars twice and now hears them as the destination.
transitions.evidence: The form analysis matches 0:20–0:35 with 0:55–1:10 (mean 0.96); the report shows a level dip at 0:50 (−14.5 dB) before the return. Score p. 3: ritardando and fermata in the last new bar, p, then the opening tune.

transitions.title: The repeat sign returns to bar nine
transitions.how: At the end of the returning tune the closing repeat sign sends the music back to bar 9. The long note that ends the eight bars gives no break; the six new bars and the fermata are heard a second time, with the opening tune again closing the strain, and the piece then ends on the same long note.
transitions.evidence: The form analysis matches 0:36–1:10 with 1:13–1:47 (lag 36.5 s, mean similarity 0.94); the report shows novelty 0.41 at 1:10. The score has a closing repeat sign at the end of bar 22.

facts: Piano with Friedrich Wieck; composition with Heinrich Dorn; extensive private study of Bach and Beethoven
Co-founder of the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik, 1834; editor until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
Leipzig Conservatoire teacher; municipal music director, Düsseldorf, 1850–53
composer.background:
Schumann grew up in Zwickau, where his father August was a bookseller and publisher. Reading and music developed together: Jean Paul’s novels, with their interruptions, doubles and changes of narrative voice, mattered alongside piano lessons. Sent to Leipzig to study law in 1828, he spent more time on music and literature; a period in Heidelberg did not reconcile him to a legal career. He returned to Leipzig to study piano seriously with Friedrich Wieck. Wieck’s daughter Clara, already performing publicly as a child, gave him an immediate example of the professional discipline he hoped to acquire.

A persistent problem with his right hand ended the prospect of a virtuoso career. The familiar account of a finger-strengthening device leaves the injury’s medical cause uncertain. Composition and criticism became his principal occupations. The early published piano works already had distinct literary and formal premises: the Abegg Variations derive a theme from letters, while Papillons relates its dances to the masked-ball ending of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre. The miniatures’ sudden juxtapositions recreate the experience of a narrative changing speakers and levels.
composer.epithet: His music lets remembered fragments, concealed names and competing inner voices interrupt the forms that contain them.
